title: Scripture also requires repentance as a condition of remission—not its merit
source_text: XXXI. Ac quemadmodum Scriptura frequenter asserit, nos per fidem habere remissionem peccatorum: Ita, non minus saepe, & expresse docet, resipiscentiam, & totam peccatoris conversionem ad Deum, esse conditionem, sine qua remissio peccatorum a Deo obtineri non potest, & quae, non minus quam fides, ad illam praeexigitur, licet illam nec efficiat, neque promereatur. Quo pertinet illud Solomonis jam antea citatum, Qui abscondit scelera sua non prosperabitur, qui autem confessus fuerit, & reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur. Et quod dicit Christus apud Lucam, Nisi resipiscatis, omnes similiter peribitis. Unde est quod Petrus sic Judaeos hortatur, Poenitentiam agite, & baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi in remissionem peccatorum. Act. 2. v. 38. Et, Poenitemini & convertimini, ut deleantur peccata vestra. Act. 3. v. 19.
pass_a_gloss: And just as Scripture frequently asserts that we have remission of sins through faith: so no less often and expressly it teaches that repentance and the sinner's whole conversion to God is a condition without which remission of sins cannot be obtained from God, and which no less than faith is prerequisite to it—though it neither effects nor merits it. To this belongs Solomon's word already cited: Whoever conceals his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy. And what Christ says in Luke: Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Hence Peter so exhorts the Jews: Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38). And: Repent and turn, that your sins may be blotted out (Acts 3:19).
pass_b_english: Repentance is as truly a gospel prerequisite of remission as faith—without meriting it.
Solomon, Christ, and Peter tie blotting out of sins to confessing, forsaking, and turning.

choices.why: Condition of remission, not its meritorious cause.
